claim: When rRNA repeats are masked, Malat1 is the second most highly bound lncRNA by Ago2.
source: When the same analysis was repeated with rRNA repeats masked, Malat1 was the second most highly bound transcript (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by AHC sequencing data after masking rRNA repeats.

claim: The largest AHC peak in Malat1 contains an 8-mer seed-binding sequence for the miR-15/16 family.
source: miRTarget, the custom miRNA-binding prediction algorithm (Liu and Wang, 2019), identified an 8-mer seed-binding sequence of the miR-15/16 family centered within the most densely bound region of the called peak (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by computational prediction using miRTarget algorithm and AHC peak data.

claim: Ago2 binding to the miR-15/16 site in Malat1 is absent in miR-15/16Δ/Δ T cells.
source: In the absence of miR-15/16, Ago2 binding to Malat1 was preserved throughout the whole transcript except for the peak containing the predicted miR-15/16 8-mer seed-binding sequence (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by AHC data comparing WT and miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells.

claim: The miR-15/16-binding site in Malat1 is evolutionarily conserved between mouse and human.
source: Furthermore, miR-15/16 binding occurred in a region of high evolutionary conservation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment and lncLOOM conservation analysis.

claim: The corresponding region in human MALAT1 is highly enriched in AHC datasets from HEK293 cells.
source: The corresponding region containing the miR-15/16-binding site in human MALAT1 was highly enriched in two publicly available AHC datasets obtained using the 293 human embryonic kidney (HEK) cell line, consistent with Malat1 regulating miR-15/16 in a colorectal cancer cell line (Karginov and Hannon, 2013; Ji et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018; Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by publicly available AHC datasets and citation to previous work.

claim: The Malat1scr mutation reduces Ago2 binding specifically at the miR-15/16-binding site.
source: Ago2 binding was preserved across the Malat1 transcript except at the mutated miR-15/16-binding site, where AHC sequence read density was greatly reduced (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by AHC data from Malat1scr/scr cells.

claim: Malat1 expression is unchanged in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells.
source: Malat1 expression was unchanged in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells as well as in the Malat1scr/scr cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data comparing genotypes.

claim: Malat1 expression is unchanged in Malat1scr/scr cells.
source: Malat1 expression was unchanged in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells as well as in the Malat1scr/scr cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data comparing genotypes.

claim: miR-15a is modestly decreased in Malat1scr/scr cells.
source: However, in freshly isolated mouse CD8+ T cells, miR-15b and miR-16 were unchanged and only miR-15a, a family member with lower expression, was modestly decreased in Malat1scr/scr cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by miRNA qPCR data.

claim: miR-15b is unchanged in Malat1scr/scr cells.
source: However, in freshly isolated mouse CD8+ T cells, miR-15b and miR-16 were unchanged and only miR-15a, a family member with lower expression, was modestly decreased in Malat1scr/scr cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by miRNA qPCR data.

claim: miR-16 is unchanged in Malat1scr/scr cells.
source: However, in freshly isolated mouse CD8+ T cells, miR-15b and miR-16 were unchanged and only miR-15a, a family member with lower expression, was modestly decreased in Malat1scr/scr cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by miRNA qPCR data.

claim: Malat1 and miR-15/16 do not influence each other's absolute abundance.
source: We conclude that Malat1 and the miR-15/16 family do not influence each other's absolute abundance in this setting.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq and qPCR data showing no significant changes in expression levels.

claim: Ago2 occupancy at miR-15/16 target sites increases in Malat1scr/scr cells compared to WT cells.
source: In WT cells, these sites constituted on average 3.2% of the binding in each 3′ UTR, and this figure increased to 3.4% in Malat1scr/scr cells, indicating that Ago2 occupancy preferentially increased at these sites when miR-15/16 binding to Malat1 was eliminated (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by AHC data comparing WT and Malat1scr/scr cells at predicted miR-15/16 target sites.

claim: Ago2 binding at miR-15/16 target sites is reduced by 69% in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells compared to WT.
source: As predicted, binding was greatly reduced in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells, representing, on average, 1.0% of binding to a given 3′ UTR, a 69% reduction in Ago2 binding compared to WT (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by AHC data comparing WT and miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells.

claim: The Malat1scr allele specifically affects miR-15/16 binding and not other miRNA families.
source: In contrast, no significant differences were observed for binding at predicted sites for the highly expressed miRNA families of miR-101, Let-7, miR-21, and miR-142, (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by AHC data for other miRNA families showing no changes.

claim: miR-15/16 target genes show decreased expression in Malat1scr/scr cells compared to WT.
source: In the case of WT to Malat1scr/scr cells, the distribution was shifted in favor of decreased target gene expression in the Malat1scr/scr cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and cumulative density plot analysis.

claim: miR-15/16 target genes show increased expression in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells compared to miR-15/16fl/fl.
source: In the case of miR-15/16fl/fl to miR-15/16Δ/Δ, the distribution was shifted in favor of increased target gene expression in the miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells, indicating that this gene set is relieved of miRNA-induced repression (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and cumulative density plot analysis.

claim: 90% of miR-15/16 target genes are either downregulated in Malat1scr/scr cells or upregulated in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells.
source: Of 479 genes in the bound target list, 432 (90%) were either downregulated in Malat1scr/scr cells or upregulated in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells, compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis of target genes.

claim: 33% of miR-15/16 target genes are both increased in miR-15/16Δ/Δ and decreased in Malat1scr/scr cells.
source: Among these genes, the expression of 298 (62%) were decreased in Malat1scr/scr cells, and 294 (61%) were increased in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells, with 160 (33%) both increased in miR-15/16Δ/Δ and decreased in Malat1scr/scr cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis and Venn diagram.

claim: The Malat1:miR-15/16 circuit regulates pathways associated with growth factor and antigen receptor signaling.
source: Gene ontology enrichment analysis revealed multiple pathways associated with growth factor and antigen receptor signaling affected by the Malat1:miR-15/16 circuit in cytotoxic T cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: CD28 is a direct target of miR-15/16.
source: For example, gene expression and AHC data support direct miR-15/16 targeting of the costimulatory receptor Cd28, the alpha subunit of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (Pik3r1) and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK1), encoded by Mapk8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by AHC data showing miR-15/16-dependent binding to CD28 3' UTR and gene expression data.

claim: Pik3r1 is a direct target of miR-15/16.
source: For example, gene expression and AHC data support direct miR-15/16 targeting of the costimulatory receptor Cd28, the alpha subunit of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (Pik3r1) and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK1), encoded by Mapk8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by AHC data and gene expression data.

claim: Mapk8 (JNK1) is a direct target of miR-15/16.
source: For example, gene expression and AHC data support direct miR-15/16 targeting of the costimulatory receptor Cd28, the alpha subunit of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (Pik3r1) and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK1), encoded by Mapk8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by AHC data and gene expression data.

claim: AHC detects a prominent miR-15/16-dependent peak in the CD28 3' UTR.
source: AHC in WT cells detected a prominent peak in the CD28 3′ UTR at the TargetScan predicted binding site for miR-15/16. This peak was absent in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells, whereas other binding peaks were preserved, empirically verifying that this binding event is miR-15/16 dependent.
evidence: Supported by AHC data comparing WT and miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells.

claim: Ago2 binding at the CD28 miR-15/16 site is modestly increased in Malat1scr/scr cells compared to WT.
source: AHC in Malat1scr/scr cells indicated a modest increase in Ago2 binding at this site compared to WT cells relative to Ago2 binding in the whole 3′ UTR (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by AHC data comparing WT and Malat1scr/scr cells.

claim: CD28 protein expression is decreased in Malat1scr/scr mice.
source: Flow cytometric measurement in primary splenic CD8+ T cells revealed that CD28 protein expression was decreased in Malat1scr/scr mice and enhanced in miR-15/16Δ/Δ mice (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring CD28 mean fluorescence intensity.

claim: CD28 protein expression is enhanced in miR-15/16Δ/Δ mice.
source: Flow cytometric measurement in primary splenic CD8+ T cells revealed that CD28 protein expression was decreased in Malat1scr/scr mice and enhanced in miR-15/16Δ/Δ mice (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring CD28 mean fluorescence intensity.

claim: CD28-responsive genes are downregulated in Malat1scr/scr cells stimulated with αCD3 alone.
source: Importantly, the Malat1:miR-15/16 circuit affected this gene set in the ɑCD3 alone condition, with Malat1scr/scr cells exhibiting decreased expression compared to WT cells, and miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells exhibiting increased expression compared to miR-15/16fl/fl cells (Figure 3E, G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and cumulative density plot analysis.

claim: CD28-responsive genes are upregulated in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells stimulated with αCD3 alone.
source: Importantly, the Malat1:miR-15/16 circuit affected this gene set in the ɑCD3 alone condition, with Malat1scr/scr cells exhibiting decreased expression compared to WT cells, and miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells exhibiting increased expression compared to miR-15/16fl/fl cells (Figure 3E, G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and cumulative density plot analysis.

claim: The effect of the Malat1:miR-15/16 circuit on CD28-responsive genes is preserved but reduced when CD28 is directly engaged.
source: This trend was preserved, but to a lesser degree, in the ɑCD3 and ɑCD28 conditions (Figure 3F, H).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and cumulative density plot analysis.

claim: Malat1:miR-15/16 interaction and CD28 signaling additively induce costimulation-responsive genes.
source: Thus, Malat1:miR-15/16 interaction and engagement of CD28 signaling additively induced costimulation-responsive genes.
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of RNA-seq data showing samples group by both genotype and stimulation condition.

claim: CD69 expression is decreased in Malat1scr/scr cells at 2 hours post stimulation.
source: CD69 exhibited decreased expression in Malat1scr/scr cells at both 2 and 4 hr post stimulation (2 hr: p = 0.0014 and 4 hr: p = 0.0598) and increased expression in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells at 4 hr post stimulation only (p < 0.0001) (Figure 4A, B), in accordance with costimulation-responsive gene module expression (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring CD69 mean fluorescence intensity.

claim: CD69 expression is decreased in Malat1scr/scr cells at 4 hours post stimulation.
source: CD69 exhibited decreased expression in Malat1scr/scr cells at both 2 and 4 hr post stimulation (2 hr: p = 0.0014 and 4 hr: p = 0.0598) and increased expression in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells at 4 hr post stimulation only (p < 0.0001) (Figure 4A, B), in accordance with costimulation-responsive gene module expression (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring CD69 mean fluorescence intensity.

claim: CD69 expression is increased in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells at 4 hours post stimulation.
source: CD69 exhibited decreased expression in Malat1scr/scr cells at both 2 and 4 hr post stimulation (2 hr: p = 0.0014 and 4 hr: p = 0.0598) and increased expression in miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells at 4 hr post stimulation only (p < 0.0001) (Figure 4A, B), in accordance with costimulation-responsive gene module expression (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring CD69 mean fluorescence intensity.

claim: Nur77 expression is unchanged across Malat1scr/scr, WT, and miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells.
source: There was no difference, however, in expression of Nur77 across Malat1scr/scr, WT, and miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells, indicating that TCR signals were equivalent (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring Nur77 mean fluorescence intensity.

claim: miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells produce significantly more IL-2 after αCD3 stimulation with or without αCD28.
source: In line with previous findings in LCMV-infected mice (Gagnon and Ansel, 2019), miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells made significantly more IL-2 and TNFɑ after ɑCD3 stimulation both with and without ɑCD28, with a trend toward increased IFNγ as well (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data measuring cytokine secretion and citation to previous work.

claim: miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells produce significantly more TNFα after αCD3 stimulation with or without αCD28.
source: In line with previous findings in LCMV-infected mice (Gagnon and Ansel, 2019), miR-15/16Δ/Δ cells made significantly more IL-2 and TNFɑ after ɑCD3 stimulation both with and without ɑCD28, with a trend toward increased IFNγ as well (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data measuring cytokine secretion and citation to previous work.

claim: Malat1scr/scr cells show a trend toward decreased IL-2 production after αCD3 + αCD28 stimulation.
source: Malat1scr/scr cells stimulated with ɑCD3 + ɑCD28 exhibited a reciprocal trend specifically for IL-2 (23% decrease compared to WT, p = 0.26) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data measuring IL-2 secretion.

claim: Malat1scr/scr mice have reduced effector memory T cells in the spleen at steady state.
source: Malat1scr/scr mice had normal naive and central memory T cell populations, but a reduced percentage and number of effector memory (CD44+CD62L–) cells in the spleen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from unchallenged mice.

claim: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells have similar numbers to WT P14 cells in the spleen at day 7 post LCMV infection.
source: The total numbers of P14 cells were similar in recipients of transferred WT or Malat1scr/scr P14 cells in both the spleen and liver at day 7, and in the spleen at day 31.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data counting transferred P14 cells.

claim: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells have similar numbers to WT P14 cells in the liver at day 7 post LCMV infection.
source: The total numbers of P14 cells were similar in recipients of transferred WT or Malat1scr/scr P14 cells in both the spleen and liver at day 7, and in the spleen at day 31.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data counting transferred P14 cells.

claim: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells have similar numbers to WT P14 cells in the spleen at day 31 post LCMV infection.
source: The total numbers of P14 cells were similar in recipients of transferred WT or Malat1scr/scr P14 cells in both the spleen and liver at day 7, and in the spleen at day 31.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data counting transferred P14 cells.

claim: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells are reduced in the liver at day 31 post LCMV infection.
source: However, there was a reduction in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells in the liver at day 31 (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data counting transferred P14 cells.

claim: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells preferentially display a KLRG1+ CD127- terminally differentiated effector memory phenotype.
source: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells preferentially displayed a phenotype associated with terminally differentiated effector memory cells (t-TEM), defined by KLRG1 expression and lack of CD127 expression as shown by Milner et al., 2020, and a corresponding reduction in the percentage of KLRG1− CD127+ memory cells (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data and citation to previous work defining t-TEM phenotype.

claim: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells have a reduced percentage of KLRG1- CD127+ memory cells.
source: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells preferentially displayed a phenotype associated with terminally differentiated effector memory cells (t-TEM), defined by KLRG1 expression and lack of CD127 expression as shown by Milner et al., 2020, and a corresponding reduction in the percentage of KLRG1− CD127+ memory cells (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells have proportionally more CD27- CD43- cells at day 31 post LCMV infection.
source: Consistent with increased KLRG1+ CD127− t-TEM cells there were proportionally more CD27− CD43− cells in both the spleen and liver at day 31 among the Malat1scr/scr transferred cells compared to WT (Figure 5G, I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells have reduced numbers of CD43+ CD27+ cells at day 31 post LCMV infection.
source: The proportional differences we observed were primarily driven by a reduction in the number of CD43+ CD27+ Malat1scr/scr P14 cells compared with wild-type P14 cells (45% reduction in liver (p = 0.0058), 30% reduction in spleen (p = 0.113)) (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: The effect of the Malat1scr allele is epistatic to miR-15/16.
source: To test whether the effect of the Malat1scr allele was epistatic to miR-15/16, we bred Malat1scr/scr to miR-15/16Δ/Δ mice to generate triple mutant Malat1scr/scr miR-15/16Δ/Δ mice. The poly-clonal LCMV response in these mice phenocopied that of miR-15/16Δ/Δ with a WT allele of Malat1, indicating that the observed effects of the Malat1scr allele are epistatic to miR-15/16 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from triple mutant mice showing they phenocopy miR-15/16Δ/Δ mice.

claim: miR-15/16Δ/Δ mice generate similar numbers of antigen-specific T cells as miR-15/16fl/fl mice during LM-GP33 infection.
source: In contrast to the increased antigen-specific CD8+ T cell numbers in LCMV-infected miR-15/16Δ/Δ mice (Gagnon and Ansel, 2019), we observed similar cell numbers in LM-GP33-infected miR-15/16Δ/Δ and miR-15/16fl/fl mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data and citation to previous work.

claim: miR-15/16Δ/Δ antigen-specific cells have decreased percentages of CD127- KLRG1+ t-TEMs during LM-GP33 infection.
source: However, the effect on memory cell differentiation was still present with decreased percentages of CD127− KLRG1+ t-TEMs and increased percentages of CD127+ KLRG1− memory cells (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: miR-15/16Δ/Δ antigen-specific cells have increased percentages of CD127+ KLRG1- memory cells during LM-GP33 infection.
source: However, the effect on memory cell differentiation was still present with decreased percentages of CD127− KLRG1+ t-TEMs and increased percentages of CD127+ KLRG1− memory cells (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: Malat1scr/scr and WT P14 cells accumulate to similar numbers in the spleen and liver at days 7 and 31 following LM-GP33 infection.
source: Transferred Malat1scr/scr and WT P14 cells accumulated in the spleen and the liver to similar numbers at both days 7 and 31 following LM-GP33 infection (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data counting transferred P14 cells.

claim: There is no change in the proportion or number of CD127- KLRG1+ Malat1scr/scr P14 cells at day 7 in the spleen or liver during LM-GP33 infection.
source: In contrast to LCMV, there was no change in the proportion or number of CD127− KLRG1+ Malat1scr/scr P14 cells at day 7 in the spleen or liver (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: KLRG1+ cells are increased in proportion and numbers in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells in the spleen at day 31 post LM-GP33 infection.
source: On day 31, KLRG1+ cells were increased in proportion and numbers in the Malat1scr/scr P14 cells (Figure 6N).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: CD127+ KLRG1- memory cells are unaffected in proportion and number in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells at day 31 post LM-GP33 infection.
source: Surprisingly, this effect was restricted to the KLRG1+ populations, as CD127+ KLRG1− memory cells were unaffected in proportion and number in both the spleen and liver (Figure 6O).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: CD43- CD27- t-TEMs are proportionally increased in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells at day 31 post LM-GP33 infection.
source: In both organs CD43− CD27− t-TEMs were proportionally increased and CD43+ CD27+ memory cells were proportionally decreased in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells (Figure 6P, Q).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: CD43+ CD27+ memory cells are proportionally decreased in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells at day 31 post LM-GP33 infection.
source: In both organs CD43− CD27− t-TEMs were proportionally increased and CD43+ CD27+ memory cells were proportionally decreased in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells (Figure 6P, Q).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: Bcl2 expression is reduced in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells in the CD43- CD27- population at day 31 during LCMV infection.
source: Bcl2 expression in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells was reduced at day 31 in the CD43− CD27− population in both LCMV and LM-GP33 infection, and also in CD43+ CD27+ cells in LCMV infection (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring Bcl2 mean fluorescence intensity.

claim: Bcl2 expression is reduced in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells in the CD43- CD27- population at day 31 during LM-GP33 infection.
source: Bcl2 expression in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells was reduced at day 31 in the CD43− CD27− population in both LCMV and LM-GP33 infection, and also in CD43+ CD27+ cells in LCMV infection (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring Bcl2 mean fluorescence intensity.

claim: Bcl2 expression is reduced in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells in the CD43+ CD27+ population at day 31 during LCMV infection.
source: Bcl2 expression in Malat1scr/scr P14 cells was reduced at day 31 in the CD43− CD27− population in both LCMV and LM-GP33 infection, and also in CD43+ CD27+ cells in LCMV infection (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring Bcl2 mean fluorescence intensity.

claim: Increased proportions of dead Malat1scr/scr cells are observed in both KLRG1+ and KLRG1- cell fractions at day 7 during LM-GP33 infection.
source: Also consistent with reduced Bcl2 expression, increased proportions of dead Malat1scr/scr cells were observed in both the KLRG1+ and KLRG1− cell fractions at day 7 during LM-GP33 infection (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data measuring dead cell percentages.

claim: A lower proportion of Malat1scr/scr P14 cells produce IL-2 when stimulated ex vivo on day 7 during LCMV infection.
source: Corroborating our in vitro observations, a lower proportion of Malat1scr/scr P14 cells produced IL-2 when stimulated ex vivo on day 7 in both infection models (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data using IL-2 capture assay.

claim: A lower proportion of Malat1scr/scr P14 cells produce IL-2 when stimulated ex vivo on day 7 during LM-GP33 infection.
source: Corroborating our in vitro observations, a lower proportion of Malat1scr/scr P14 cells produced IL-2 when stimulated ex vivo on day 7 in both infection models (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data using IL-2 capture assay.

claim: Malat1scr/scr P14 cells produce equivalent amounts of IL-2 at day 31 after infection with either LCMV or LM-GP33.
source: Higher proportions of memory cells were able to produce IL-2 ex vivo at day 31 after infection with either LCMV or LM-GP33 infection, and Malat1scr/scr P14 cells produced equivalent amounts of IL-2 (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data using IL-2 capture assay.

claim: miR-15/16 are a widely and highly expressed tumor suppressor miRNA family important for cell proliferation and survival.
source: miR-15/16 is a widely and highly expressed tumor suppressor miRNA family important for cell proliferation and survival.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: miR-15/16 play important roles in T cell responses to viral infection, including the regulation of antigen-specific T cell expansion and memory.
source: miR-15/16 play important roles in T cell responses to viral infection, including the regulation of antigen-specific T cell expansion and memory.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Malat1 was first identified as highly expressed in both malignant tumors and healthy lung and pancreas with high interspecies conservation.
source: Malat1 was first identified as highly expressed in both malignant tumors and healthy lung and pancreas with high interspecies conservation (Ji et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Malat1 is mostly localized to the nucleus, where it is found within nuclear speckles.
source: Malat1 is mostly localized to the nucleus, where it is found within nuclear speckles, although it is not necessary for their formation (Nakagawa et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Malat1 is not necessary for nuclear speckle formation.
source: Malat1 is mostly localized to the nucleus, where it is found within nuclear speckles, although it is not necessary for their formation (Nakagawa et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Malat1 is actively regulated during cytotoxic T cell differentiation with higher expression in memory precursors and lower expression in short-lived effector cells during LCMV infection.
source: Malat1 is actively regulated during cytotoxic T cell differentiation with higher expression in memory precursors and lower expression in short-lived effector cells during LCMV infection (Kakaradov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: T cells stimulated in vitro express decreased levels of Malat1 over time.
source: Similarly, T cells stimulated in vitro express decreased levels of Malat1 over time (Masoumi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Early reports using large genetic deletions in the mouse Malat1 locus detected widespread gene expression changes but failed to identify a role for Malat1 in mouse development or cytotoxic T cell responses.
source: Early reports using large genetic deletions in the mouse Malat1 locus detected widespread gene expression changes but failed to identify a role for Malat1 in mouse development or cytotoxic T cell responses (Nakagawa et al., 2012; Yao et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2012), though a recent report using RNAi detected altered T cell responses (Kanbar et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A recent report using RNAi detected altered T cell responses involving Malat1.
source: Early reports using large genetic deletions in the mouse Malat1 locus detected widespread gene expression changes but failed to identify a role for Malat1 in mouse development or cytotoxic T cell responses (Nakagawa et al., 2012; Yao et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2012), though a recent report using RNAi detected altered T cell responses (Kanbar et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CD28 costimulation is essential for IL-2 production, memory cell formation, and memory recall responses in vivo.
source: CD28 costimulation is essential for IL-2 production, memory cell formation, and memory recall responses in vivo (Borowski et al., 2007; Eberlein et al., 2012; Fuse et al., 2008; Grujic et al., 2010; Suresh et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IL-2 is required in a CD8+ T cell-intrinsic manner for the formation of CD127+ KLRG1- memory cells.
source: IL-2 is also essential for these same processes and in particular is required in a CD8+ T cell-intrinsic nature for the formation of CD127+ KLRG1− memory cells (Blattman et al., 2003; Kahan et al., 2022; Pipkin et al., 2010; Toumi et al., 2022; Whyte et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Bcl2 is the first characterized target of miR-15/16.
source: The pro-survival protein Bcl2 is the first characterized target of miR-15/16 (Cimmino et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Higher abundance of Bcl2 in memory cells aids their survival and persistence.
source: Higher abundance of Bcl2 in memory cells (as compared with short-lived effector cells) aids their survival and persistence, counteracting their increased expression of pro-apoptotic factors such as Bim (Kurtulus et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IL-2 is critical for the induction of Bcl2 in memory T cells to promote their survival.
source: IL-2 is critical for the induction of Bcl2 in memory T cells to promote their survival (Toumi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IL-2 production by cytotoxic T cells predisposes them to differentiate into a memory phenotype, likely by an autocrine/paracrine mechanism.
source: Furthermore, IL-2 production by cytotoxic T cells predisposes them to differentiate into a memory phenotype, likely by an autocrine/paracrine mechanism (Kahan et al., 2022; Kurtulus et al., 2011; Wojciechowski et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Listeria monocytogenes infection induces lower expression of multiple costimulatory ligands compared to LCMV, making the antigen-specific response more sensitive to ablation of CD28 costimulation.
source: Compared to LCMV, Listeria monocytogenes (LM) infection induces lower expression of multiple costimulatory ligands so the antigen-specific response is more sensitive to the ablation of CD28 costimulation (Welten et al., 2015).
